title: Beyond
summary: Seventh chords, arpeggios, chord-tone soloing, modes, secondary dominants, and reading standard notation.

lessons.title: Seventh chords
lessons.summary: Add a seventh to triads: major 7th, dominant 7th, minor 7th, and half-diminished chords, and the seven diatonic seventh chords.

steps.title: Four notes
steps.body:
A **seventh chord** adds one more third on top of a triad: the seventh. Four common types:

| Type | Formula | Example | Symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| major 7th | 1 3 5 7 | C E G B | Cmaj7 |
| dominant 7th | 1 3 5 b7 | G B D F | G7 |
| minor 7th | 1 b3 5 b7 | A C E G | Am7 |
| half-diminished | 1 b3 b5 b7 | B D F A | Bm7b5 (Bø7) |

"7" means a major seventh (11 half steps) only in "maj7". A plain "7" is always the minor seventh (10 half steps). The **diminished seventh chord** (1 b3 b5 bb7, such as Bdim7 = B D F Ab) also exists; it comes from the harmonic minor.

steps.title: Diatonic seventh chords
steps.body:
Stack four notes on each degree of C major:

**Cmaj7 – Dm7 – Em7 – Fmaj7 – G7 – Am7 – Bm7b5**

In numerals: **Imaj7 – ii7 – iii7 – IVmaj7 – V7 – vi7 – viiø7**. Only V gets a dominant 7th, which is why the chord has that name. The ii7–V7–Imaj7 progression (Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 in C) is the core of jazz harmony.

In G: Gmaj7 – Am7 – Bm7 – Cmaj7 – D7 – Em7 – F#m7b5.

steps.title: Open fingerings
steps.body:
- **Cmaj7**: the C chord with finger 1 lifted (string 2 open = B). Strum 5–1.
- **Dm7**: finger 2 on string 3 fret 2, finger 1 barres strings 2 and 1 at fret 1. Strum 4–1.
- **G7**: finger 3 on string 6 fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 fret 2, finger 1 on string 1 fret 1. Strum all six.
- **Am7**: the Am chord with finger 3 lifted (string 3 open = G). Strum 5–1.
- **Em7**: finger 2 on string 5 fret 2 only (string 4 open = D). Strum all six.
- **Bm7b5**: string 5 fret 2, string 4 fret 3, string 3 fret 2, string 2 fret 3. Mute strings 6 and 1.

steps.title: Four qualities
steps.caption: Cmaj7, C7, Cm7, Cm7b5, all from C.

exercise.prompt: Play Cmaj7, Dm7, G7, Am7, Em7.

mistakeTips: Cmaj7 and Am7 are easy: they are C and Am with one finger lifted.
Dm7: flatten finger 1 across strings 2 and 1.
The open strings carry the 7ths. Keep them ringing.

exercise.prompt: ii–V–I in C: Dm7, G7, Cmaj7, one minute.

mistakeTips: Dm7 to G7: finger 1 stays at fret 1 but moves from strings 2-1 to string 1 only.
G7 to Cmaj7: the F on string 1 drops to E (open) as the chord resolves. Listen for it.

questions.prompt: Spell G7.
Spell Fmaj7.
Which diatonic seventh chord falls on degree 5 of a major key?
What is the vii chord in G major as a seventh chord?
How does Am7 differ from Am?

reviewItems.answer: Cmaj7 Dm7 Em7 Fmaj7 G7 Am7 Bm7b5

lessons.title: Arpeggios
lessons.summary: Play chords one note at a time as melodic lines, in open position and in a movable fingering.

steps.title: Chords as lines
steps.body:
An **arpeggio** is a chord played one note at a time, and for a soloist it is a map of the safest notes over that chord. Every note of an arpeggio is a **chord tone**.

Practicing arpeggios through a progression trains your hands to find each chord's notes as the chords change. That is the skill chord-tone soloing depends on (next lesson).

steps.title: Through a progression
steps.body:
In open position, over **C – Am – Dm – G7** (I – vi – ii – V7 in C), play four chord tones per chord, lowest first:

- **C**: C (5 fret 3), E (4 fret 2), G (3 open), C (2 fret 1)
- **Am**: A (5 open), E (4 fret 2), A (3 fret 2), C (2 fret 1)
- **Dm**: D (4 open), A (3 fret 2), D (2 fret 3), F (1 fret 1)
- **G7**: G (6 fret 3), B (5 fret 2), D (4 open), F (4 fret 3)

steps.title: C – Am – Dm – G7 arpeggios
steps.caption: Four notes per chord, eighth notes.

playback.rhythm: e e e e e e e e e e e e e e e e

exercise.prompt: Arpeggiate C, Am, Dm, G7: four notes each, in time.
exercise.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q q

mistakeTips: Hold each chord fingering while you pick its notes.
Change fingerings during the last note of each group, not after it.
Pick each note once, cleanly. Let them ring into each other.

steps.title: A movable minor arpeggio
steps.body:
Inside position 1 of A minor pentatonic (Stage 6) sits the A minor arpeggio: A C E. Leave out D and G and you get:

string 6: 5 (A), 8 (C) · string 5: 7 (E) · string 4: 7 (A) · string 3: 5 (C) · string 2: 5 (E) · string 1: 5 (A), 8 (C)

Slide it to any fret for other minor chords: at fret 7 it is B minor, at fret 10 D minor.

exercise.prompt: A minor arpeggio, position 1, up and down.

mistakeTips: One note per string except strings 6 and 1.
Use finger 1 at fret 5 and finger 3 at fret 7; finger 4 at fret 8.

questions.prompt: What notes are in a G7 arpeggio?
questions.explanation: The four chord tones of G7.

questions.prompt: Why practice arpeggios through a progression?
choices: To find each chord's tones as the chords change
questions.explanation: They map the chord tones for soloing.

questions.prompt: The A minor arpeggio fingering moved to fret 10 gives…

reviewItems.answer: A chord's notes played one at a time.

lessons.title: Chord-tone soloing
lessons.summary: Aim for notes of the current chord on strong beats so your lines follow the changes.

steps.title: Follow the chords
steps.body:
Pentatonic soloing uses one scale over the whole song. **Chord-tone soloing** changes targets with each chord: on strong beats (1 and 3), play a note that belongs to the chord of the moment. Between those beats, any scale note can connect them.

The strongest targets are the **guide tones**, the 3rd and 7th of each chord. They decide major or minor and dominant or not, and they usually move by a half or whole step to the next chord's guide tones.

steps.title: A line over C – Am – F – G
steps.body:
Each measure starts on the chord's 3rd:

- **C**: E D C E (E is the 3rd of C)
- **Am**: C B A C (C is the 3rd of Am)
- **F**: A G F A (A is the 3rd of F)
- **G**: B D G (B is the 3rd of G)
- **C**: C

Notice the first notes of each measure: E, C, A, B, C. A smooth line that spells the harmony even without chords.

steps.title: The line with its chords
steps.caption: Chords first, then the line alone.

exercise.prompt: Play the chord-tone line in time: E D C E | C B A C | A G F A | B D G(half) | C(whole).
exercise.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q q q h w

mistakeTips: All notes are in open position: F (4 fret 3), G (3 open), A (3 fret 2), B (2 open), C (2 fret 1), D (2 fret 3), E (1 open).
Feel how the first note of each measure matches the chord change.

exercise.prompt: Improvise over C – Am – F – G for one minute. Start each measure on a note of the new chord.

mistakeTips: C = C E G, Am = A C E, F = F A C, G = G B D.
Try landing on the 3rd of each chord: E, C, A, B.
Leave space; a few well-placed chord tones beat a flood of notes.

questions.prompt: Over an F chord, which note is a chord tone?
What are the guide tones of G7?
Over Am, which of these is the 3rd?
questions.explanation: A to C is a minor third.

lessons.title: Modes
lessons.summary: Hear the seven modes of the major scale, and play Dorian and Mixolydian over vamps.

steps.title: Same notes, new home
steps.body:
A **mode** is what you get when you play a scale from a different starting note and treat that note as home. You already know one case: A natural minor is C major started on A.

The seven modes of C major (the **parent scale**):

| Degree | Mode | From C major | Compared with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Ionian** | C to C | the major scale itself |
| 2 | **Dorian** | D to D | minor with a raised 6 |
| 3 | **Phrygian** | E to E | minor with a b2 |
| 4 | **Lydian** | F to F | major with a #4 |
| 5 | **Mixolydian** | G to G | major with a b7 |
| 6 | **Aeolian** | A to A | natural minor itself |
| 7 | **Locrian** | B to B | minor with b2 and b5 |

steps.title: Why the home note matters
steps.body:
D Dorian and C major contain the same notes, but they do not sound the same. What decides the mode is the **home note and the chords underneath**. Over a Dm chord, the notes of C major sound like D Dorian; over C, they sound like C major.

So compare each mode to the major or minor scale on the **same** root. That shows its one characteristic note:

- **Dorian** = minor + natural 6. D Dorian: D E F G A **B** C. The B (instead of Bb) is its bright color.
- **Mixolydian** = major + b7. G Mixolydian: G A B C D E **F**. The F (instead of F#) gives a bluesy, rock sound.
- **Lydian** = major + #4: dreamy. **Phrygian** = minor + b2: dark and Spanish-sounding.

steps.title: Vamps
steps.body:
Modes are easiest to hear over a **vamp**, a short repeating chord pattern:

- **Dorian vamp**: Dm7 to G (i7 to IV). The G chord contains B, the Dorian 6th.
- **Mixolydian vamp**: G to F (I to bVII). The F chord contains F, the Mixolydian b7.

Many folk tunes are modal. "Scarborough Fair" and "Drunken Sailor" are both Dorian; you will play the second one in the review.

steps.title: Dorian, then Mixolydian
steps.caption: D Dorian over Dm7, then G Mixolydian over G.

exercise.prompt: D Dorian, one octave, open position: D (string 4 open) to D (string 2 fret 3).

mistakeTips: These are the C major notes, starting from D.
Lean on the B (string 2 open): it is the Dorian color note.

exercise.prompt: G Mixolydian, one octave: G (string 6 fret 3) to G (string 3 open).

mistakeTips: Same fingering as G major except F natural: string 4 fret 3 instead of fret 4.

exercise.prompt: Improvise with D Dorian over a Dm7–G vamp for one minute.

mistakeTips: End phrases on D.
Use B over the G chord to bring out the Dorian sound.

questions.prompt: Which mode starts on degree 5 of the major scale?
questions.explanation: Ionian 1, Dorian 2, Phrygian 3, Lydian 4, Mixolydian 5, Aeolian 6, Locrian 7.

questions.prompt: Dorian is natural minor with which change?
What is the parent major scale of E Dorian?
questions.explanation: Dorian starts on degree 2; E is degree 2 of D major.

questions.prompt: Spell G Mixolydian.
choices: G A B C D E F
G A B C D E F#
G A Bb C D E F
questions.explanation: G major with F instead of F#.

questions.prompt: Which mode is the same as the natural minor scale?

reviewItems.prompt: Order of the modes from degree 1?
reviewItems.answer: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian.

reviewItems.prompt: Characteristic note of Mixolydian compared with major?
Characteristic note of Dorian compared with natural minor?

lessons.title: Secondary dominants
lessons.summary: Borrow dominant 7th chords to lead strongly into chords other than I.

steps.title: Five of five
steps.body:
V7 pulls strongly to I because its 3rd (the leading tone) rises a half step to the tonic. You can use the same pull toward any major or minor chord in the key by putting **that chord's** V7 in front of it. This is a **secondary dominant**.

In C major:

| Target | Its V7 | Written | Note outside the key |
|---|---|---|---|
| G (V) | D7 | V7/V | F# |
| Am (vi) | E7 | V7/vi | G# |
| Dm (ii) | A7 | V7/ii | C# |
| Em (iii) | B7 | V7/iii | D# |
| F (IV) | C7 | V7/IV | Bb |

"V7/V" is read "five of five". The note outside the key is the borrowed leading tone; it rises a half step into the target's root.

steps.title: Hearing it
steps.body:
Compare C – Dm – G7 – C with C – **A7** – Dm – G7 – C. The A7 adds C#, which pushes up to D. The move from a secondary dominant to its target is a **resolution**, a release of tension.

Chains of dominants are common in ragtime and early jazz: E7 – A7 – D7 – G7 – C, each resolving down a fifth to the next.

diagram.caption: A7: the C# (3rd) leads to D.

steps.title: With and without
steps.caption: C Dm G7 C, then C A7 Dm G7 C.

exercise.prompt: C – A7 – Dm – G7, one measure each, four downstrokes.

mistakeTips: A7 to Dm: finger 2 moves from string 4 to string 3, both at fret 2.
Listen for the C# in A7 (string 2, fret 2) rising to D in Dm (string 2, fret 3).

exercise.prompt: V7/vi to vi: E7 to Am, one minute.

mistakeTips: E7 is E with finger 3 lifted. Move fingers 1 and 2 over one string for Am, then add finger 3.
The G# (string 3 fret 1 in E7) rises to A (string 3 fret 2 in Am).

questions.prompt: In C major, what is V7/V?
questions.explanation: V of C is G; the V7 of G is D7.

questions.prompt: In G major, what is V7/vi?
questions.explanation: vi of G is Em; the V7 of E is B7.

questions.prompt: Which note in E7 is outside C major?
questions.explanation: E G# B D. G# is the leading tone of A.

questions.prompt: Where does A7 usually resolve in C major?

reviewItems.prompt: Secondary dominants in C major: V7/V, V7/vi, V7/ii?

reviewItems.answer: The V7 of a chord other than I, placed before it.

lessons.title: Reading standard notation
lessons.summary: Read notes on the treble staff, connect them to the fretboard, and sight-read a short line.

steps.title: The staff
steps.body:
Standard notation writes pitch on a **staff**: five lines and four spaces. Higher on the staff means higher in pitch. Guitar music uses the **treble clef**, which curls around the second line from the bottom and marks it as G.

- **Lines**, bottom to top: **E G B D F** ("Every Good Boy Does Fine").
- **Spaces**, bottom to top: **F A C E** (spells "face").

Notes above or below the staff use short **ledger lines**. The key signature and time signature come right after the clef.

diagram.caption: Treble staff lines: E G B D F.

steps.title: Guitar sounds an octave lower
steps.body:
To keep notes on the staff, **guitar music is written one octave higher than it sounds**. The clef sometimes has a small 8 underneath to say so.

| Written | Sounds | Where |
|---|---|---|
| E below three ledger lines (E3) | E2 | string 6 open |
| C on one ledger line below (C4) | C3 | string 5 fret 3 |
| E, bottom line (E4) | E3 | string 4 fret 2 |
| G, second line (G4) | G3 | string 3 open |
| B, middle line (B4) | B3 | string 2 open |
| E, top space (E5) | E4 | string 1 open |

So the open strings are easy anchors: G string = second line, B string = middle line, high E = top space.

steps.title: Rhythm on the staff
steps.body:
Note heads show pitch; the rest of the symbol shows length. Hollow head with no stem = whole note; hollow with stem = half; filled with stem = quarter; a flag or beam = eighth. You already count these from Stage 2.

Tab shows where to play; notation shows pitch and rhythm exactly. Reading both lets you use any written music, including piano and vocal parts.

diagram.caption: Written pitch. Guitar sounds one octave lower.

exercise.prompt: Sight-read this line in open position. The diagram shows the written notes; play them one octave lower, as guitarists always do.
exercise.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q w

mistakeTips: Bottom line E = string 4 fret 2. Second line G = open string 3. Middle line B = open string 2.
Space C (third space) = string 2 fret 1. Space A (second space) = string 3 fret 2. Space F (first space) = string 4 fret 3.
Look one note ahead of the one you are playing.

questions.prompt: What are the lines of the treble staff, bottom to top?
What are the spaces, bottom to top?
A note on the middle line is written B4. Which open string plays it?
questions.explanation: It sounds B3: the open B string.

questions.prompt: Why is guitar written an octave higher than it sounds?
choices: To keep notes on the treble staff
questions.explanation: Otherwise most notes would need many ledger lines.

steps.title: Name the note on the staff

reviewItems.answer: Lines E G B D F; spaces F A C E.

reviewItems.prompt: How does written guitar music relate to sounding pitch?
reviewItems.answer: Written one octave higher than it sounds.

lessons.title: Beyond review: modes and sevenths
lessons.summary: Review seventh chords, modes, secondary dominants, and reading, then play a Dorian folk tune and a ii–V–I progression.

steps.title: What you know now
steps.body:
- Seventh chords: **maj7, 7, m7, m7b5**; diatonic sevenths Imaj7 ii7 iii7 IVmaj7 V7 vi7 viiø7.
- **Arpeggios** and **chord-tone soloing** follow the changes.
- **Modes**: same notes, new home. Dorian = minor + 6; Mixolydian = major + b7.
- **Secondary dominants** borrow V7 to lead into any diatonic major or minor chord.
- Treble staff: lines E G B D F, spaces F A C E; guitar sounds an octave lower than written.

questions.prompt: Spell Dm7.
In D major, what is V7/V?
questions.explanation: V of D is A; the V7 of A is E7.

questions.prompt: Which mode is major with a #4?
questions.explanation: F Lydian: F G A B C D E, with B instead of Bb.

questions.prompt: What is the parent scale of A Dorian?
questions.explanation: A is degree 2 of G major.

questions.prompt: What is the iii7 chord in C major?

steps.title: Drunken Sailor
steps.body:
"Drunken Sailor" is a traditional sea shanty and is in the public domain. It is in **D Dorian**: the second line sits on a C chord, and the third line climbs A B C D. That B natural is the Dorian 6th.

All notes are in open position: D (4 open), E (4 fret 2), F (4 fret 3), G (3 open), A (3 fret 2), B (2 open), C (2 fret 1 or 5 fret 3), high D (2 fret 3).
